object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged event representing something broken that is tracked through resolution.

source_references.excerpt: Something breaks. We find out about it, one way or another. Somebody declares an incident, somebody runs it, we fix it, we write it up.
Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique, never reused? ... Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal, automated or manually raised, indicating something may be wrong, sourced from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.
Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Customer Ticket
object_types.definition: A ticket raised by or on behalf of a customer reporting a problem, from the support ticketing system.

source_references.excerpt: Or a customer tells us and monitoring never fires, which is the embarrassing one.
And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: The technical impact / blast-radius classification of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: The customer-urgency classification of an incident, independent of severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Which is completely different... Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: Incident State
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can act as an incident commander.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A standing organizational group that owns one or more services.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system or capability that can be affected by incidents and is owned by a team.

source_references.excerpt: And an incident affects a service? ... Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

populations.description: Example scenario illustrating severity/priority independence: Halberd Financial outage.

source_references.excerpt: Halberd Financial goes down -- one customer, one region, our biggest account, contractual penalties. That's a P1 all day. It's a SEV3.

populations.description: Example scenario: Sunday marketing site outage was SEV1 but low priority.

source_references.excerpt: We had a SEV1 at four in the morning on a Sunday where the affected surface was the marketing site. Everything down, nobody awake, no revenue impact. That was a P4.

source_references.excerpt: That was a P4.

ambiguities.description: Whether the 'monitoring' status some staff use informally between mitigated and resolved should be treated as a real state is contested; the facilitator excludes it because it isn't in the system dropdown, but Owen insists people treat it as a state in practice.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... That's not a state, that's a thing people write in the channel. ... People treat it as a state. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is used ambiguously in practice to mean either the incident commander (a temporary role) or the service owner (a standing team assignment); the transcript flags this as a recurring real-world collision even though the model distinguishes the two clearly.

source_references.excerpt: Now -- the other "owner." ... And in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: The term 'sev' is colloquially used by staff to refer to either severity or priority, causing real confusion, even though the two are modeled as independent, uncorrelated fact types.

source_references.excerpt: And people say "sev" when they mean either. Somebody says "we've got a sev one" in a channel and I don't know whether to page the whole platform team or ring one account manager.

ambiguities.description: Whether duplicate-of chains (transitive duplicate links) are actually forbidden or merely undesirable is unclear: the rule against chains is described as 'the rule as intended' but explicitly 'not enforced' in the system, and two-deep chains have been observed. It's ambiguous whether this should be modeled as a hard constraint or left as a data-quality issue.

source_references.excerpt: But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Whether incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is is explicitly undecided and deferred to a stakeholder (Ravi) outside this session; no 'cause classification' concept exists in the current model despite being discussed at length.

source_references.excerpt: Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether an incident can have more than one alert or more than one customer ticket linked as origin (the transcript establishes at-least-one-of is required, and gives an example of 'three tickets' associated with one alert-triggered incident, but never states a maximum), so the multiplicity of the origin relationships beyond 'at least one of alert-or-ticket' is unresolved.

source_references.excerpt: Or both, which is the common one -- the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.

ambiguities.description: The final exchange (Kit saying he'd already left the call ten minutes earlier) is a humorous aside about call reliability and not a modeling point, but it underscores that Kit's attention/reliability during the session (and thus the completeness of his input) may be uncertain -- a soft caveat on the trustworthiness of his late contributions about duplicates.

source_references.excerpt: Then I've got what I need, and Kit can go back to his offsite. ... I've been back at the offsite for ten minutes, I just left this on.
